instructions: Edit this file to update every measured figure on the site. Do not add a number unless it is in the resume or in a committed result file in the project's repository. The home page, case studies, and tables all read from here. Each project has one headline stat (headline.stat), three short facts (factIds), and a short caveat. Search this file for the old value and update every place it appears, including caveat text.

projects.title: Deep Portfolio Constructor
projects.purpose: A neural network that builds a long-only portfolio for long-term wealth, trained on the growth of wealth after every trading cost.
projects.proves: Trained only on the growth of wealth, the network turned $1 in 1960 into $1,368, against $929 for the market: +0.58% a year, a gap the pre-registered test cannot tell from luck (t = 1.40).
projects.summary: A transformer that allocates across Kenneth French's 30 US industries, trained in PyTorch on the growth of wealth itself through a differentiable simulator of buying, holding and paying to trade, walk-forward from 1960 and tested out of sample against the market and five classical long-only strategies.
projects.caveat: Out of sample from January 1960 to September 2026 (801 months), long-only, fully invested, every trade costs 10 bps. The test, the comparisons and the decision rule were pre-registered in git before the network was run out of sample; against the market the verdict is no detectable difference (Newey-West t 1.40, 95% interval −0.07% to +1.50% a year). Kenneth French's 30 US industry portfolios hold every listed firm at each date, so there is no survivorship bias among firms, but they are industries, not funds an investor could buy in 1960, and the features are ones finance research found later. A simple momentum tilt grew +0.96% a year above the market (t 2.93). US data only: one country's century is still one history.

image.alt: Growth of $1 invested in January 1960 for seven long-only strategies, on a log scale.

headline.qualifier: Long-only, out of sample from January 1960, net of 10 bps per trade. Holding the market grew to $929; the difference is +0.58% a year: no detectable difference, by the pre-registered test.

projects.title: Pension Lab
projects.purpose: What it costs to keep a pension promise funded for 20 years, and whether a policy learned by simulation does better than the rule plans use. In simulation it does; on real history it is not detectably different from that rule.
projects.summary: A pension plan that is 90% funded has promised inflation-indexed payments for 60 years. Its liability is valued off the 10-year yield with expected inflation; its assets are stocks, 10-year bonds and bonds matched to the promise. Four standard policies (60/40, liability-driven, fully matched, a glide path) are compared with a policy trained in PyTorch through a differentiable simulator of the plan, on what the plan costs its sponsor over 20 years and how bad that gets.
projects.proves: In 10,000 simulated futures the learned policy costs the sponsor $5.0 per $100 promised against $9.9 for a glide path, and $30.2 against $69.1 in the worst 5%: better by the pre-registered test. When yields never return to an average it is better than the glide path, and over 34 real 20-year periods it is not detectably different from it.
projects.caveat: Pre-registered in git before the test ran. A stylised plan: one yield for all maturities, expected inflation is the last ten years' average, no inflation-linked bonds, no credit or private assets, no longevity risk. Simulated futures rearrange US history from 1953 and are the model the learned policy was trained on: against the glide path the verdict there is better (score difference −43.8, 95% interval −46.9 to −40.7). On futures in which yields never return to an average, without retraining: $7.0 against $14.1, better. On 34 real 20-year periods, which overlap and amount to about three independent ones: $6.3 against $6.3, no detectable difference. US data only.

headline.qualifier: Average of 10,000 simulated futures; a glide path costs $9.9. Against it the pre-registered verdict is better in simulation, better when yields never return to an average, and no detectable difference on real history.

projects.learned: It holds less in stocks than the glide path whether the plan is short or funded. Above all it follows the yield: the higher the yield, the more it puts in bonds matched to the promise.
projects.tuned: The network still costs less than the tuned rule in simulation, so tuning is not the whole story.
projects.why: Most of the simulated saving came from patterns in the last twelve months that hold inside the runs of history the simulator replays. A plan cannot rely on them: real history, where every network had seen only the past, gave the same answer.
projects.stress: The same rise in rates can hurt or help a pension plan, depending on why it happened.
projects.stressBand: Both moves are inside their bands: the two channels are of similar size, so the net is small and these estimates do not settle its sign.

projects.title: World Shock Lab
projects.summary: Event studies of Federal Reserve, Bank of Canada, and OPEC surprises across global assets, with a pre-registered test of whether machine learning adds anything, and forecasts published before each decision.
projects.caveat: Machine learning did not beat the linear model on the average move in either pre-registered study. Quantile boosting won only on 5% tail pinball loss. None of 80 regime tests survived false-discovery control.

projects.summary: A decoder-only transformer pretrained from scratch in PyTorch. On the test split, patch_s2, one seed, 97 configurations: CRPS 0.688× upstream AutoARIMA, 95% CI [0.624, 0.757], better. Validation CRPS was 0.605× Seasonal Naive.
projects.caveat: patch_s2 on the test split, one seed, 97 configurations: CRPS 0.688× upstream AutoARIMA, 95% CI [0.624, 0.757], better. Its validation CRPS was 0.605× Seasonal Naive, 16 configurations, one seed. A smaller CPU model (833,440 parameters, 3 seeds, 97 configurations) was scored once on the test split: CRPS 1.109× Seasonal Naive, no detectable difference, and 1.217× AutoARIMA, worse.

projects.title: Aurvane
projects.summary: The trust layer for the agent economy. Each agent bot carries a signed mandate; every action passes four rules, helper bots only ever get narrower mandates, held actions wait for your Allow or Deny, and everything lands in a hash-chained log. Against a simulated agent that obeys every injected instruction, attacks that landed fell from 30 of 30 to 7 of 30. A red team of 12 smarter attacks: 8 contained, 2 capped by the budget, 2 get through, shown on purpose.
projects.purpose: Every agent action, signed, bounded, visible. An agent may read anything, but untrusted text can never choose where money or data goes.
projects.proves: Untrusted text cannot steer an agent's money or data. Against a simulated agent that obeys every injection, attacks that landed fell from 30 of 30 to 7 of 30, and money lost from 12,135 CAD to 135 CAD.
projects.caveat: Simulated worst-case agent that obeys every injected instruction, 60 paired tasks (30 clean, 30 poisoned), deterministic, run once. The numbers measure the guard, not a model. The 7 attacks that still land are by design: 4 rewrite a cover letter (Aurvane guards actions, not prose) and 3 add a 45 CAD charge at a store the human already trusts, capped by the signed budget. Real-model runs (Claude, Grok, Qwen) use the same harness, capped at 5 USD, and have not been run yet.
